fixes.title: A form that asks enough to have a real first conversation

data.label: Links that go nowhere
data.evidence: none among the 12 links we read
data.why: A link that goes nowhere reads as a broken site to the person who clicks it.

data.label: Links pointing at a development address
data.evidence: none
data.why: A link to localhost or a staging host takes the visitor to a browser error page with your name on it.

data.label: Links back to your own http address
data.evidence: every link to your own pages stays on https
data.why: A link to the http:// spelling of your own address makes the visitor ask for the page in the clear before your redirect sends them back, and costs them a round trip to do it.

data.label: Links that say where they go
data.evidence: all 12 links we read name their destination
data.why: “Read more” tells a visitor nothing, and with no aria-label behind it, it is the whole label a screen reader announces when it lists the links on your page.

data.label: Phone links a phone can dial
data.evidence: no tel: links on the pages we read
data.why: A tel: link that is not a number does nothing at all when it is tapped.

data.label: Social links that go to your accounts
data.evidence: none left unedited
data.why: An unedited theme placeholder sends a visitor to a login page or to somebody else entirely.

data.label: Navigation that agrees with itself
data.evidence: 4 shared menu items go to the same place on every page
data.why: The same menu item leading to two different pages is the kind of confusion visitors blame on you rather than on the menu.

data.label: Placeholder Latin left in the copy
data.evidence: none across the 3 pages we read
data.why: Lorem ipsum on a live page tells a visitor the site was never finished.

data.label: Theme placeholder text left in the copy
data.evidence: none across the 3 pages we read
data.why: “Your text here” on a live page reads as a site nobody has looked at since it was built.

data.label: Template code showing as text
data.evidence: none across the 3 pages we read
data.why: A visitor sees the machinery instead of the sentence, which reads as broken rather than unfinished.

data.label: Text with broken characters
data.evidence: none across the 3 pages we read
data.why: Apostrophes and quotes rendering as â€™ is the most visible sign of a migration nobody checked, and it is a one-line fix at the source.

data.label: Pages that say they are unfinished
data.evidence: no page announces itself unfinished, across the 3 we read
data.why: A live page announcing it is coming soon is a page better unlinked until it is not.

data.label: Your name in the page title
data.evidence: “Acme Roofing — Commercial Roof Repair in Boise, Idaho”
data.why: The title is the line in a search result, a browser tab and a shared link. Without your name in it, all three are anonymous.

data.label: A headline on every page
data.evidence: all 1 pages carry one
data.why: The h1 is the page's headline. A page without one gives a reader — and an assistant looking for something to quote — nothing that says what the page is about.

data.label: One headline, not a list of them
data.evidence: no page marks more than two of its lines as the headline, across the 1 we read
data.why: When everything on the page is marked as the page's headline, none of it is, and whatever gets quoted back is whichever one came first in the markup.

data.label: Headlines that say what the page is about
data.evidence: every headline describes its page
data.why: A headline that is only your company name describes none of the page below it.

data.label: A different headline on each page
data.evidence: only one page was read, so there is nothing to compare it with
data.why: Identical headlines make every page look like the same page, to a reader scanning tabs and to a search engine choosing which one to show.

data.label: Your business details in structured data
data.evidence: your LocalBusiness block is missing url, logo
data.why: This is the block an assistant reads to learn who you are. Half-filled, it answers half the question and the rest gets taken from a directory you do not control.

data.label: Your address and hours in structured data
data.evidence: missing telephone, openingHours
data.why: A local business block without an address, a phone or opening hours is the one an assistant will fill in from elsewhere.

data.label: Structured data pointing at this site
data.evidence: no such block in your structured data
data.why: A structured-data url pointing at a domain you no longer use tells every assistant that reads it to go and look somewhere else.

data.label: One phone number, everywhere
data.evidence: no telephone in your structured data
data.why: When the number in your structured data is not the number on your page, an assistant may quote either one.

data.label: Ratings you publish about yourself
data.evidence: no review or rating markup on this site
data.why: Google does not show star ratings a business publishes about itself, so the markup does nothing but sit there.

data.label: Pages search engines are allowed to list
data.evidence: none of the 3 pages we read asks to be hidden
data.why: This one line tells every search engine and assistant to leave the page out of their results entirely. It is almost always left over from a staging site, and nothing on the page looks wrong.

data.label: Links search engines are allowed to follow
data.evidence: no page-wide nofollow
data.why: It tells search engines not to follow any link on the page, so nothing you link to gets credit from it.

data.label: A declared character set
data.evidence: declared on all 3 pages
data.why: Without a declared character set the browser guesses, and a wrong guess is what turns apostrophes into â€™.

data.label: Titles that survive a search result
data.evidence: all 1 are between 10 and 70 characters
data.why: A title that is too long is cut off mid-word in the result, and one that is too short wastes the most valuable line you get.

data.label: Descriptions that survive a search result
data.evidence: all 1 are between 40 and 200 characters
data.why: The description is the sentence under your link. Too long and it is truncated; too short and the engine writes its own.

data.label: A share image with a full web address
data.evidence: https://acme.example/og.jpg
data.why: A relative og:image renders no card at all on Slack, LinkedIn or iMessage — the link arrives as bare text.

data.label: A different description on each page
data.evidence: fewer than two pages carry a description, so there is nothing to compare
data.why: Identical descriptions make every page look like the same page in a search result, and the engine usually replaces them with a sentence of its own choosing.

data.label: An icon for the browser tab
data.evidence: no icon is declared, so we fetched /favicon.ico instead — reported below
data.why: Without one the browser shows a blank page icon in the tab and the bookmark, which is the smallest possible thing to fix and the most often seen.

data.label: Pages that point at themselves
data.evidence: 1 of 3 point at their own page; the other 2 name a page they duplicate
data.why: A canonical naming another page tells search engines to index that page instead of this one. That is right for a genuine duplicate, and the fastest way to remove real pages from search results when it is not.

data.label: Canonicals that stay on your domain
data.evidence: every canonical stays on this domain
data.why: A canonical on another domain hands every page's search ranking to that domain. It is usually a staging host or a site they used to own.

data.label: Language alternates that name themselves
data.evidence: this site publishes no language alternates
data.why: An hreflang set that does not name itself is ignored, so the translated pages compete with each other instead of being offered to the right reader.

data.label: Fields typed for a phone keyboard
data.evidence: no enquiry form on the pages we read, which is reported separately
data.why: An email field typed as plain text gives a phone the ordinary keyboard, so the visitor hunts for the @ at exactly the moment they had decided to write to you.

data.label: Fields a phone can fill in one tap
data.evidence: no enquiry form on the pages we read, which is reported separately
data.why: With these, a phone offers to fill the whole form in one tap. Without them it does not offer at all.

data.label: A form that does not put answers in the URL
data.evidence: no enquiry form on the pages we read, which is reported separately
data.why: A form that submits with GET puts everything the visitor typed into the address bar, and from there into your server logs and their browser history.

data.label: A form that posts somewhere we recognise
data.evidence: no enquiry form on the pages we read, which is reported separately
data.why: A form posting to an endpoint nobody owns any more looks like it worked and silently goes nowhere.

data.label: Fields marked as required
data.evidence: no enquiry form on the pages we read, which is reported separately
data.why: Without it the browser cannot stop a half-filled form being sent, and the visitor finds out something was missing only if somebody tells them.

data.label: Pages without JavaScript errors
data.why: A script that throws stops running, so whatever it was doing — a menu, a form, a gallery — silently stops working for every visitor from that point on.

data.label: Files the page asks for and gets
data.why: A file the page asks for and does not get is a missing image, an unstyled section or a feature that does nothing.

data.label: Pages that fit a phone screen
data.why: Something on the page is wider than a phone screen, so the whole page scrolls sideways. Most of your visitors are on a phone, and this is the first thing they will notice.

data.label: Text big enough to read
data.why: Text under twelve pixels is uncomfortable on a desktop and unreadable on a phone without pinching.

data.label: Images sized for where they are shown
data.why: These images are downloaded at several times the size they are shown at, so every visitor pays for pixels they never see.

data.label: An SPF record, so your email is trusted
data.evidence: v=spf1 include:_spf.example -all
data.why: Without it, anyone can send email that appears to come from your address, and your own mail is more likely to be filed as spam.

data.label: A DMARC record, so SPF is enforced
data.evidence: no record at _dmarc.acme.example
data.why: SPF says who may send as you. DMARC is what tells the receiving mail server to act on that, and to report attempts to you. Without it the first one is advisory.

data.label: A mail server for your domain
data.evidence: mx.acme.example
data.why: There is no mail server listed for your domain, so email sent to any address at it is rejected.

data.label: An email address that can receive mail
data.evidence: the addresses you publish are on your own domain, which is checked above
data.why: The address you publish is on a domain with no mail server, so anything sent to it bounces.

data.label: A domain registration with room to spare
data.why: Registration dates are public; whether it renews automatically is not, so this is one to confirm at your registrar rather than a fault we can see. When a registration does lapse the site and the email stop together, usually on a weekend, and getting them back is neither quick nor certain.

data.label: A favicon that actually loads
data.evidence: no icon at /favicon.ico
data.why: The icon in the browser tab and the bookmark bar. When the file is missing the tab shows a blank sheet, which is the difference between a site that looks maintained and one that does not.

data.label: http:// reaching https:// without a detour
data.evidence: http:// does not end up on https://
data.why: Somebody typing your address without https, or following an old link, should land on the secure version in one step. Every extra redirect is delay on the first impression, and a chain that ends on http means the page is served in the clear.

data.label: A homepage that answers the same way twice
data.evidence: two requests, both 200
data.why: Two requests seconds apart got different answers, which is what an overloaded or half-deployed server looks like from outside. Some visitors are seeing the bad one.

data.label: One address per page, slash or no slash
data.evidence: /services — both forms answer with no canonical to settle which is the real one
data.why: When /about and /about/ both answer with the same page and neither says which is real, search engines index both and split the credit between them.

data.label: A homepage that lives at one address
data.evidence: /index.html — it answers with the homepage's content and does not point back at it
data.why: Your homepage answers at two addresses. Links, shares and search results scatter across both instead of accumulating on one.

data.label: Paths that do not answer to two spellings
data.evidence: /Services — it answers as its own page, so the same content has two addresses
data.why: The same page answers at two spellings, so the same content competes with itself in search results.

data.label: A sitemap whose pages still exist
data.evidence: there is no sitemap to check, which is covered above
data.why: A sitemap is a list you hand to search engines saying 'these pages exist'. Entries that no longer answer waste the crawl budget you were trying to direct.

data.label: Outbound links that still work
data.evidence: the one outbound link answers
data.why: A link on your site that leads nowhere is a dead end for the visitor and a small mark against the page for a search engine.

data.label: A share image that loads
data.evidence: the share image loads
data.why: This is the picture that appears when your page is shared in a message, on LinkedIn, or in a Slack channel. When the file does not load, the share renders as a bare grey box.

data.label: A share image big enough to render
data.evidence: the homepage declares no share image, which is covered above
data.why: A share image under 200 pixels on either edge is either cropped to nothing or dropped entirely by the platform showing it.

data.label: A logo that loads
data.evidence: the first image on the homepage loads
data.why: A logo that does not load leaves a broken-image icon at the top of every page, and it is the first thing on the page.

data.label: Internal links that go straight there
data.evidence: 2 internal links, none redirecting twice
data.why: A link that redirects more than once makes every visitor wait through each hop, and search engines pass less credit along a chain than a direct link.

data.label: A form that catches an empty submission
data.evidence: we did not try a form on this run
data.why: Somebody who taps send too early should be told what is missing. A form that submits anyway puts a blank enquiry in your inbox and tells them it worked, so they never follow up and you have nothing to follow up on.

data.label: A form that catches a mistyped email
data.evidence: we did not try a form on this run
data.why: A mistyped address is the one mistake that costs you the whole enquiry: the message arrives, and there is no way to answer it. Catching it while the visitor is still on the page is the only chance to fix it.

data.label: Telling browsers to always use https
data.evidence: no strict-transport-security header
data.why: Without it, the first visit of the day can still be made over plain http before the redirect happens.

data.label: A policy for what may run on your pages
data.evidence: no content-security-policy header
data.why: It is the difference between a compromised script running on your site and being blocked by the browser.

data.label: Stopping browsers guessing file types
data.evidence: no x-content-type-options header
data.why: One line that prevents a browser treating an uploaded file as something executable.

data.label: Stopping other sites framing yours
data.evidence: no x-frame-options header
data.why: Without it, anyone can put your site inside theirs and collect what visitors type into it.

data.label: Declaring what your pages may ask for
data.evidence: no permissions-policy header
data.why: It limits what code running on your own pages may ask visitors for — including code you did not write, if a dependency is ever compromised.

data.label: Not leaking more of your addresses than the browser already does
data.evidence: no referrer-policy header, so the browser's own default applies — which does not leak the address
data.why: Browsers already trim the page address to your bare domain before handing it to a site a visitor clicks through to. Two values of this header undo that and send the whole address, query string included.

data.label: Not advertising your software versions
data.evidence: no version numbers in your response headers
data.why: Naming the exact version you run tells anyone looking which published vulnerabilities to try first.

data.label: Pages sent compressed
data.evidence: your HTML is served uncompressed
data.why: Uncompressed HTML is roughly four times the bytes for the same page, paid for by every visitor on a phone.

data.label: An https policy that lasts
data.evidence: no strict-transport-security header to read a max-age from
data.why: A max-age of a few minutes gives almost none of the protection the header exists for.

data.label: robots.txt not blocking your whole site
data.evidence: nothing site-wide is disallowed
data.why: A blanket Disallow tells every search engine and every assistant to stay off the whole site. It is usually left over from a staging server.

data.label: robots.txt naming your sitemap
data.evidence: no Sitemap: line in robots.txt
data.why: Naming the sitemap in robots.txt is how a crawler that has never seen your site finds the list of your pages.

data.label: A sitemap that lists your pages
data.evidence: this site has no sitemap.xml
data.why: A sitemap listing fewer pages than your own navigation links to leaves the rest to be found by luck.

data.label: A file written for AI assistants
data.evidence: no llms.txt — recorded, not counted against you, because no engine has published that it reads one
data.why: A short llms.txt states, in your own words, what you do and which pages matter. No answer engine has published that it reads one, so this is recorded rather than counted against you.

data.label: Something measuring whether any of this works
data.evidence: no third-party analytics on the pages we read
data.why: Without any analytics you cannot tell whether a change helped, which visit turned into an enquiry, or whether the work was worth doing.
